text: `&` and `&&` produce the same result for boolean operands, differing only in efficiency.
explanation: They produce the same result only when evaluating the right side is safe and free of effects. `d != 0 & n / d > 2` throws where the `&&` version returns false, because `&` evaluates both sides. Short-circuiting is a difference in *which code runs*, not in speed, and the idiom `x != null && x.foo()` depends on it entirely.
